content:
The short answer Parquet is a storage format — it’s designed to sit on disk (or S3) efficiently.
Arrow is an in-memory format — it’s designed to move data between systems without copying.
You’ll often use both: read a Parquet file into an Arrow table, process it in memory, write it back as Parquet.
Parquet Parquet is a columnar file format. Because it stores data column-by-column rather than row-by-row, it compresses extremely well and lets query engines skip entire columns they don’t need.
import pyarrow.parquet as pq table = pq.read_table("data/sales.parquet", columns=["date", "revenue"]) Good for:
Long-term storage Files on S3, GCS, HDFS Query engines like DuckDB, Spark, Athena Arrow Arrow defines a language-agnostic in-memory columnar layout. The point is zero-copy reads — a Python process and a Rust process can share the same Arrow buffer without serialising.
import pyarrow as pa table = pa.table({"x": [1, 2, 3], "y": [4.0, 5.0, 6.0]}) Good for:
Passing data between processes (IPC) Flight (Arrow’s gRPC-based data transfer protocol) Avoiding pandas’ memory overhead When you need both import pyarrow.parquet as pq # Read from disk into Arrow in-memory table table = pq.read_table("sales.parquet") # Process in Arrow (zero-copy column access) revenue = table.column("revenue") # Write back pq.write_table(table, "sales_processed.parquet")

title: Arrow vs Parquet: When to Use Which

content:
Why dataclasses Before @dataclass (added in Python 3.7), a simple data-holding class meant writing __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ by hand. Dataclasses generate all of that for you.
from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass class Pipeline: name: str schedule: str enabled: bool = True That’s it. You get a constructor, a readable repr, and equality comparison for free.
Defaults and default factories from dataclasses import dataclass, field @dataclass class Pipeline: name: str tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list) # mutable default — must use field() The default_factory pattern catches people out: you can’t write tags: list = [] because the same list object would be shared across all instances.
When to use Pydantic instead Dataclasses don’t validate types at runtime — if you pass enabled="yes" it won’t complain. Reach for Pydantic when:
You’re parsing external input (API responses, config files) You need coercion or validators You want .model_dump() / .model_json_schema() For internal data passing where the types are under your control, dataclasses are lighter and have zero dependencies.
summary:
Why dataclasses

Before @dataclass (added in Python 3.7), a simple data-holding class meant writing __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ by hand. Dataclasses generate all of that for you.

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Pipeline:
    name: str
    schedule: str
    enabled: bool = True

That’s it. You get a constructor, a readable repr, and equality comparison for free.

Defaults and default factories

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Pipeline:
    name: str
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)  # mutable default — must use field()

The default_factory pattern catches people out: you can’t write tags: list = [] because the same list object would be shared across all instances.
title: Python Dataclasses: A Practical Guide

Ingredients Marinade
700g chicken thighs, cut into chunks 150g full-fat yoghurt 1 tsp kashmiri chilli powder 1 tsp garam masala 1 tsp cumin 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste Salt Sauce
2 tbsp butter 1 tbsp oil 2 medium onions, roughly chopped 4 garlic cloves 1 inch ginger 400g tinned tomatoes 1 tsp kashmiri chilli powder 1 tsp coriander powder 150ml double cream 1 tsp sugar Salt Method Mix the marinade ingredients with the chicken and leave for at least 2 hours (overnight is better). Grill or cook in a hot dry pan until charred at the edges. Set aside.
Fry the onions in butter and oil on medium heat until deeply golden — about 20 minutes. Add garlic and ginger, cook 2 more minutes.
Add tomatoes and spices, simmer 15 minutes. Blend smooth. Pass through a sieve if you want restaurant-level texture.
Return to the pan, add the chicken and cream. Simmer 10 minutes. Adjust salt and add sugar to balance the tomato acidity.
Serve with basmati rice or naan.
Notes The char on the chicken matters — it gives the sauce some depth. Don’t skip it.
summary:
Ingredients

Marinade

  • 700g chicken thighs, cut into chunks
  • 150g full-fat yoghurt
  • 1 tsp kashmiri chilli powder
  • 1 tsp garam masala
  • 1 tsp cumin
  • 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste
  • Salt

Sauce

  • 2 tbsp butter
  • 1 tbsp oil
  • 2 medium onions, roughly chopped
  • 4 garlic cloves
  • 1 inch ginger
  • 400g tinned tomatoes
  • 1 tsp kashmiri chilli powder
  • 1 tsp coriander powder
  • 150ml double cream
  • 1 tsp sugar
  • Salt

Method

  1. Mix the marinade ingredients with the chicken and leave for at least 2 hours (overnight is better). Grill or cook in a hot dry pan until charred at the edges. Set aside.
title: Butter Chicken

content:
Ingredients 1 tin Heinz baked beans 2 thick slices white bread (Warburtons or similar) Salted butter Optional: a splash of Worcestershire sauce, pinch of smoked paprika Method Toast the bread. While still hot, butter generously — the butter should melt into the bread completely.
Heat the beans in a small saucepan on medium-low. Stir occasionally. If using Worcestershire sauce, add it now.
When the beans are steaming (not boiling — boiling makes them watery), pour over the toast.
Dust with smoked paprika if you like.
Notes The ratio is important. One tin between two slices is the correct amount. Any less and it’s dry. Any more and the toast goes soggy before you finish.
summary:
Ingredients

  • 1 tin Heinz baked beans
  • 2 thick slices white bread (Warburtons or similar)
  • Salted butter
  • Optional: a splash of Worcestershire sauce, pinch of smoked paprika

Method

  1. Toast the bread. While still hot, butter generously — the butter should melt into the bread completely.

  2. Heat the beans in a small saucepan on medium-low. Stir occasionally. If using Worcestershire sauce, add it now.

  3. When the beans are steaming (not boiling — boiling makes them watery), pour over the toast.
title: Proper Beans on Toast
